questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: To learn the language and hear Japanese 24/7. Also of course to explore their culture.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Kyoto and not Tokyo. I didn't want to live in the capital where it's busy 24/7 but in a rather smaller city. Best believe, Kyoto was big enough. Where we lived was quiet, but in no time with public transportation were we in city centre.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: One thing I/we need to remember is that we were there for studying. It was very tough regarding homework, assignments, etc. My hours also doubled at the university from the semester before to the semester in Japan. It wasn't my first time in Japan and I didn't have the urge to travel the whole country since I've seen most of the most touristy spots before. But all my energy went to studying, which is a bit sad to think about. I made friends in class and the dorm, which I'm happy about. The times where I relaxed and enjoyed myself were also good and fun, with or without friends.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I would say it was easy, but then again, not when everything is so different. We got a lot of help from our dormitory supporters, and without them we would probably be behind in all the papers we needed to fill out. There is a lot of paperwork to be done.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The most assistance was from our dormitory supporters. If we were unsure or had any questions, we could always ask them. They were the real lifesavers over there. I'm very grateful to them.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The R-Globe office and our dormitory supporters worked together and their welcoming with news and all the stuff we needed to do helped us alot.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I don't know if it was "on campus", but the dormitory was offered through the R-globe office, which was right next to our campus. The location of the dormitory is similar to that of Tietgen and Sindrecampus. The first question we got from our home university regarding our semester in Japan was if we wanted to live in their dormitories. We agreed to live in the dormitories; however, months later, just two days before the application form closed, we were unexpectedly reminded to sign up for them. It was weird and irritating. We took the last rooms that were available and weren't able to apply however we wanted, we could only take whatever was left.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: The dormitory had shared kitchens. But you had to buy your own pots and pans, dishwashing soap, etc. Former attendants donated their kitchen appliances so we got our stuff from there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: If you're used to living in shared housing it should be fine. But they have strict rules about visitors, which can seem odd to us europeans. No one was allowed to enter your room and outside visitors had to sign a paper with name and date and could only stay in the "public area" in our dorm until 21 o'clock in the evening. If that's something they care about, then maybe they should look to find their own place.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Sadly, not everyone is as clean or neat as I am, so the toilets, shower rooms, and kitchen could get very ugly at times which happened a lot and sucked. It wasn't the dormitories fault, but the other exchange students fault.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The paperwork for going on an exchange is a lot. Every time you think you're done there is always a bit more somewhere. I also observed that they have a preference for questionnaires, which is acceptable; however, how many of these are necessary? My number is 2 on the scale right before, mainly because it's time-consuming. It is a lot and can be confusing. But it was done in the end

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: In all their papers or forms they say you can write to them; I don't think I did that except once. The response time was late.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I attended the classes I chose and was successful in that.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Our home university requires a level of Japanese that most of us can't be on when leaving for Japan. We tried that level and after six days the teachers put us down to a lower level saying we were not good enough. Compared to the other students in that higher level class, even if we wanted to, we were not on their level. In my understanding, if that doesn't change, a way to maybe save it and avoid the "reeksamen" is for you to chose "special kanji" class as an course. The ways they teach in Denmark and in Japan are so different, that may be why we were not good enough, or we simply put just weren't good enough.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was good. The courses I chose were also good. But the courses were relative few for a BA. If I could, I would have chosen business courses, but those were only offered to MA students.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of my BA courses were good and on par with the courses at our home university.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In the Japanese classes it was very different; they spoke only Japanese, which was difficult at first, but at the end we understood, and it helped us a lot. Our teachers were very nice. The other courses were in English and fascinating. The level was appropriate, and teachers were good.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: mandatory Japanese classes, Japanese Society, Japanese Media and Arts, and Post-Colonialism.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Post-Colonialism was very interesting and I would recommend it if you like history/international relations. Japanese Media and Arts for those who like manga and anime.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: National Health insurance and pension. We didn't need to pay the pension since we were only there for 1 month. But the NHI we had to pay.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Compared to Denmark, it is very cheap to live in Japan

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't look for clubs or anything, so I don't think I can answer this. But I know they had a lot of events going on.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of them I think.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Can't say anything about it.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If you have time, go out to eat or explore other cities or tourist places.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The Japanese students in your dormitory and in your classes may be a breeze to talk to. It can be easy to find new friends/connections. The R-globe office also has some events, and also a lot of other organisations will be introduced to you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In the beginning, it can be difficult to remember all rules, but it will come to you right away.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: maybe the part where eating or shopping or doing stuff alone is normal. A small detail that is quite nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. remember you're there to study! It is tough! 2. Travel if you can 3. Don't hesitate to ask for help

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of small details or information I can think of; I would gladly help them with the application and paperwork

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My level of understanding Japanese. Without me knowing, I suddenly understood a lot.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I would say the paperworks sometimes. But you can overcome it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: For the future students, I would gladly lend my help. A lot of work has to be done before going, and a lot of small details can be mentioned before going.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
